voice_profile: Natural mature British male medical teacher. Conversational, thoughtful, unhurried and slightly informal rather than an announcer.

stages.script: Okay. So, hyponatraemia. The first thing I want you to get out of your head is the idea that a low sodium necessarily means there isn't enough sodium in the body. It might. But that's not what the blood result is actually telling you. Sodium is a concentration. It's sodium in relation to water. So imagine I keep exactly the same amount of sodium, but I add more and more water. What happens? The sodium concentration falls. Nothing has happened to the amount of sodium. I've simply diluted it. And that is the useful starting point for this whole subject. Hyponatraemia is, in many cases, much more a problem of water balance than a problem of sodium itself. Have a look at the two compartments here and play with the water. Once that makes sense, the rest becomes much easier.

Right. So why do we actually care about this? If this is true hypotonic hyponatraemia, the fluid outside the cells has become more dilute. And water moves towards the more concentrated compartment, so water moves into the cells. Now, most tissues can cope with a little bit of swelling. The brain is different because it's sitting inside the skull and there isn't much room for it to expand. So brain cells swelling is the thing we're worried about. And now the speed matters enormously. If the sodium drops quickly, the brain hasn't had time to adapt and the patient can become very unwell: headache, vomiting, confusion, seizures, coma. If it falls slowly, the brain starts getting rid of intracellular osmoles, so less water is pulled in. That's clever and protective. But it creates another problem: if you then correct a chronic hyponatraemia too quickly, water can leave those adapted brain cells too quickly. So already you can see why both the fall and the correction can be dangerous.

Now, before we start talking about SIADH and urine sodium and all of that, there is one question we have to answer first. Is this actually hypotonic hyponatraemia? Because a low sodium number doesn't automatically mean the plasma is too dilute. The classic example is hyperglycaemia. Lots of glucose outside the cells pulls water out of the cells into the extracellular space, and that water dilutes the sodium. So the sodium falls, but the plasma isn't hypotonic. And, much less commonly, very high lipids or proteins can give you pseudohyponatraemia with some laboratory methods. So don't jump from low sodium straight to SIADH. First look at serum osmolality. Is it low, normal, or high? It's the low-osmolality group that follows the usual hyponatraemia pathway we're building here.

Okay, now we get to the hormone that really makes the whole thing hang together: ADH, or vasopressin. Normally, if the plasma is becoming too dilute, ADH should switch off. That's exactly what you'd want. The collecting ducts stop reabsorbing so much water, you produce very dilute urine, and you get rid of the excess water. Fine. But ADH has another trigger, and clinically this is incredibly important: circulation. If the body thinks the effective circulating volume is falling, it releases ADH to hold on to water. So you've got two competing messages. The osmolality is saying, we're too dilute, get rid of water. But the circulation is saying, hang on, I need that water. And if the circulation is sufficiently threatened, that signal wins. That's why someone who is dehydrated can remain hyponatraemic even though, from an osmolality point of view, ADH ought to be switched off.

So how do we know whether ADH is actually having an effect? We ask the kidney. And the simplest way of doing that is the urine osmolality. If the patient is hypotonic and the urine osmolality is a hundred or less, the kidney is doing what it should do: it's making very dilute urine. In practical terms, ADH is largely switched off. So then think about situations where the patient is simply taking in more water than they can excrete, or where there is so little solute available that water excretion becomes limited. But if the urine osmolality is above a hundred, the kidney is holding on to water. ADH effect is there. And notice how the question now changes. We no longer ask, does this patient have SIADH? We ask, why is ADH switched on? That question gets you much closer to the answer.

Right. ADH is on. Why? The next useful clue is urine sodium. If the urine sodium is low, say around thirty millimoles per litre or less, the kidney is trying quite hard to conserve sodium. Why would it do that? Usually because the body thinks effective arterial volume is low. That might be genuine volume loss: vomiting, diarrhoea, dehydration, whatever. But it can also happen when there is loads of fluid in the body and the circulation is still effectively underfilled, as in heart failure or cirrhosis. If the urine sodium is higher, the kidney isn't avidly conserving sodium, and now things like SIADH, adrenal insufficiency, renal salt loss and diuretics move up the list. But don't turn thirty into some magical number. Diuretics in particular can completely mess up this interpretation. It's a clue in a physiological story, not a diagnosis by itself.

Now let's see if we can derive the causes rather than memorise a table. We've got hypotonic hyponatraemia and ADH is on. So ask: what is making the body retain water? One possibility is that the circulation genuinely is depleted: vomiting, diarrhoea, blood loss, third-space losses, renal salt loss. The body releases ADH because it wants to protect the circulation. Another possibility is that total body water is actually increased, but the effective circulation is poor: heart failure, cirrhosis, advanced renal disease. Again, ADH stays on. Then you've got the group where circulation is basically okay but ADH is still being released: SIADH, severe nausea, pain, drugs, lung disease, CNS disease. And don't forget cortisol deficiency, because that can look remarkably like SIADH. Then there is a different branch altogether: huge water intake or very low solute intake. There, ADH may be appropriately suppressed, but the kidney still can't get rid of enough free water. So rather than six lists, keep asking the same question: why can't this patient get rid of water?

This is the point where the traditional words hypovolaemic, euvolaemic and hypervolaemic become useful. I actually don't like starting with them because clinical volume assessment isn't terribly reliable and people end up memorising boxes. But once you understand the physiology, the boxes make sense. In hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, sodium and water have both been lost, but the circulation is depleted, so ADH comes on and water is retained. In euvolaemic hyponatraemia, classically SIADH, there is a relatively small excess of body water without the obvious oedema you'd expect from major fluid overload. And in hypervolaemic hyponatraemia, here's the slightly counter-intuitive bit: total body sodium may actually be increased. There is plenty of sodium in the body. But total body water has increased even more, so the measured sodium concentration is low. Again: concentration, not simply amount.

Now let's interrupt all of that physiology with a patient. Sodium is one hundred and twelve and the patient is having a seizure. At this point, the elegant diagnostic algorithm is not your first priority. The brain is. If this is severe symptomatic hypotonic hyponatraemia, cerebral oedema can be immediately dangerous, and you need controlled treatment with hypertonic saline while you're working out the cause. What you're trying to achieve initially is not a normal sodium. You're trying to raise it enough to reduce brain swelling and improve the dangerous neurological symptoms. Then you slow down and control the subsequent correction, because particularly in chronic hyponatraemia, overcorrection creates the risk of osmotic demyelination. In a child, of course, use the current paediatric emergency guideline for the exact hypertonic saline dose and correction limits. The conceptual point is simple: severe brain symptoms change the urgency.

Okay. Let's rebuild it once from the beginning. You see a low sodium. Don't ask, which list of causes do I remember? Ask four questions. First: is it genuinely hypotonic? Check the serum osmolality and think about glucose. Second: if it is hypotonic, is the kidney getting rid of water appropriately? The urine osmolality tells you that. A very dilute urine means ADH is essentially off. A concentrated urine means ADH effect is present. Third: if ADH is on, why is it on? Is the body defending the circulation? Is there renal salt loss? Is this SIADH? Is there an endocrine mimic? Use urine sodium, the history, drugs, examination and the rest of the biochemistry to answer that. And fourth, throughout all of this: is the brain in danger? How low is the sodium, how quickly did it fall, and are there neurological symptoms? If you can reason through those four questions, hyponatraemia stops being a horrible collection of lists. You can actually derive what's happening from the physiology.
